shape | SHāp | noun 1 the external form, contours, or outline of someone or something: she liked the shape of his nose | houseplants come in all shapes and sizes | chest freezers are square or rectangular in shape. • a person or thing that is difficult to see and identify clearly: he saw a shape through the mist. • a specific form or guise assumed by someone or something: a fiend in human shape. 2 a geometric figure such as a square, triangle, or rectangle. • a piece of material, paper, etc., made or cut in a particular form: stick paper shapes on for the puppet's eyes and nose. 3 the correct or original form or contours of something: her skirt had lost its shape long ago. • definite or orderly arrangement: check that your structure will give shape to your essay. 4 [with adjective] the specified condition or state of someone or something: most economists think the economy is in good shape | he was in no shape to drive | the building was in poor shape. • the distinctive nature or qualities of something: the future shape and direction of the country. verb [with object] give a particular shape or form to: most caves are shaped by the flow of water through limestone | shape the dough into two-inch balls. • make (something) fit the form of something else: [with object and infinitive] : suits have been shaped to fit so snugly that no curve is undefined. • determine the nature of; have a great influence on: his childhood was shaped by a loving relationship with his elder brother. • [no object] US English develop in a particular way; progress: the yacht was shaping well in trials. • form or produce (a sound or words). PHRASES in any way, shape, or form (also in any shape or form) in any manner or under any circumstances (used for emphasis): this definitely wasn't a normal job in any way, shape, or form, but it certainly was interesting. in shape | in ˈSHāp | in good physical condition: to play this game well, you have to be in shape | she has to work hard to keep in shape | almost anyone can exercise and get in shape. in the shape of represented or embodied by: retribution arrived in the shape of my irate father. lick someone/something into shape mainly British English take action in order to bring someone or something into a satisfactory or desired state: they advertised for a director to lick their productions into shape. out of shape | ˌoud əv ˈSHāp | 1 no longer having the correct or original form or contours: check that the pipe end and compression nut are not bent out of shape. 2 (of a person) in poor physical condition; unfit: he was overweight and out of shape. the shape of things to come the way the future is likely to develop. [the title of a novel by H. G. Wells (1933)]shape up or ship out informal, mainly North American English used as an ultimatum to someone to improve their performance or behavior or face being made to leave. take shape assume a distinct form; develop into something definite or tangible: the past few months have seen the state's health insurance legislation begin to take shape. throw shapes British English informal dance to popular music: I watched as other clubbers threw shapes on the dance floor | yours truly attempted to throw some shapes to long forgotten tunes from the 1970s. whip someone/something into shape (also knock someone/something into shape) act forcefully to bring someone or something into a satisfactory or desired state: the bank were eager to whip the company into shape for eventual sale. PHRASAL VERBS shape up | ˌSHāp ˈəp | develop or progress in a particular way: I wanted to see how things had been shaping up in my absence | it was shaping up to be another bleak year. • become physically fit: I need to shape up. • improve one's behavior or performance to the required standard: we have never been afraid to tell our children to shape up | the manager has ordered his team to shape up. DERIVATIVES shapable | ˈSHāpəb(ə)l | (also shapeable) adjective shaper | ˈSHāpər | noun ORIGIN Old English gesceap ‘external form’, also ‘creation’, sceppan ‘create’, of Germanic origin.
